TacoBoy is built on LibretroDroid, which is licensed under the GNU General Public License v3. That licence requires anyone who receives a copy of the app to be able to get its source code, so the link is here rather than buried. If the link above is not set yet, ask whoever gave you this build for the source.
TacoBoy contains no games and no BIOS files. You supply your own, from cartridges and discs you own. Nothing is downloaded for you, and the app has no way to obtain them.

TacoBoy is built almost entirely from other people’s work. Every emulator core below is a separate project with its own licence and its own authors, listed so credit lands where it belongs and so anyone redistributing this build knows what they are agreeing to. Two cores are not free for commercial use — marked below — which is one reason this app is not sold.

A summary of this device and build. If you are reporting a problem, copy this and include it — it answers the first several questions anyone would ask. It contains no personal information: device model, Android version, memory page size, app build, which emulator cores are selected, and the on-screen pad setting. If your device uses 16 KB memory pages, a copy of this is especially useful to send, even if everything works.

Rapid-fires whichever face or shoulder buttons you are holding, so you don’t have to tap. Bind a Turbo Key for the system you’re playing in the list below — then Hold means it fires only while that key is held, and Toggle means one press turns it on until you press again. Never applies to the D-pad: a repeating direction would stop your character dead between pulses rather than making it move faster. Physical controllers only; the on-screen pad has no key to bind.

The physical button that turns rapid fire on, for this system only — different consoles leave different buttons spare. Whatever you bind here stops working as its normal button while Turbo is set to Hold or Toggle, so pick one this system doesn’t use. Does nothing until Turbo above is set to Hold or Toggle.

Scales the whole on-screen pad — every button, the D-pad and the sticks together — for larger fingers or a smaller screen. Positions are unchanged, so the layout keeps its shape as it grows. For a single control that needs to be a different size from the rest, use Edit On-Screen Layout in the in-game menu and tap that control: the tweaks you make there apply on top of this. Reset On-Screen Layout clears those tweaks and leaves this setting alone.

A short tick each time an on-screen button or direction is pressed — the closest a glass button gets to the feel of a real one. Tap to cycle; each tap plays the level it selects, so you can feel the difference while choosing. Only affects the on-screen pad, never a physical controller. On phones whose motor can\'t vary strength the levels differ by length of buzz instead.
Save states are disabled while Hardcore Mode is on, per RetroAchievements\' rules. Your SRAM/cart save is unaffected. Turn this off in Settings → Achievements.

Switching cores can change which save states work for this system\'s games — your SRAM/cart save is unaffected. Takes effect the next time a game is loaded.

A filter drawn over the finished picture, separate from the renderer above. Sharp keeps upscaled pixels crisp instead of blurry; CRT adds scanlines like an old television; LCD adds the pixel grid of a handheld screen; Upscale 1-3 smooth diagonal jaggies while keeping edges sharp, getting better-looking and more expensive as the number goes up. Purely a matter of taste, and it costs a little performance. Takes effect the next time this system\'s game is loaded.

Takes effect the next time this system\'s game is loaded — it won\'t change a game already running.\n\nBeetle PSX HW\'s hardware_gl renderer scatters a few wrong-coloured pixels over some 2D artwork. It\'s a bug in the core itself rather than in TacoBoy, and it usually leaves actual gameplay alone — menus, logos and character-select screens are what it shows up on. Switching that system to software gives a clean picture, at the cost of the higher internal resolutions and texture filtering only the hardware renderer can do.

Draws each console pixel as a whole number of screen pixels instead of a fraction of one, leaving a thin border where the picture no longer reaches the edge. Without a shader that\'s a subtle sharpness difference, but it\'s what stops an LCD grid or CRT scanlines from coming out unevenly spaced or shimmering when the picture moves. The vertical is what gets snapped and the width follows it, so the aspect ratio stays as the console intended. Takes effect the next time a game is loaded.
No renderer options for the systems currently installed.
Tap a binding below, then press the physical button you want to assign. Save the result as a preset to reuse or apply to another system.

When a Pocket Taco connects, every system\'s bindings reset to these defaults — or to your starred preset, if you\'ve marked one as default below. Turn this off to keep a customized layout in place across reconnects instead.
Tap to apply to %1$s. Long-press to delete.
Per-system core options — a curated subset of what each emulator core actually exposes. Takes effect the next time this system\'s game is loaded.
Hold speeds up only while the key is held down; Toggle flips fast-forward on/off with each press. Assign a key below — nothing is bound by default.
Shows a frame-rate counter in the top corner of the game screen — useful for checking performance. Takes effect the next time a game is loaded.
When off, opening TacoBoy always shows the ROM prompt/library instead of jumping straight back into your last game — you can still resume it manually from the Library screen.
Drops frames to keep the game at full speed when your device can\'t draw every one. Modern phones don\'t need it — turn it up only if a game stutters.

Dims and warms the picture to imitate an original screen, which was far less vivid than a phone display. GBA matches the handheld; GBC matches a Game Boy Player on a TV. OFF shows the colours exactly as the game outputs them.

Blends each frame with the one before it. Some games flicker sprites on and off every frame — a trick that looked solid on the original LCD but strobes on a modern screen. The ghosting choices imitate that slow old screen more heavily.
Softens harsh high frequencies, closer to how the handheld\'s tiny speaker sounded. Purely a matter of taste.
Lets Left and Right (or Up and Down) register at once — impossible on a real D-pad. A few games have tricks that need it; leave it off otherwise.

Adds colour to original (non-colour) Game Boy games. \'auto\' uses the palette Nintendo gave that game on the Game Boy Color; GBC and SGB choose which machine\'s palette set to draw from. Disabled keeps the original green-grey look. No effect on games that were already in colour.

Which regional console to emulate. Region changes speed and screen size — PAL machines ran at 50Hz and slightly taller — and a few games only run correctly on the region they were sold in. Auto reads it from the cartridge and is almost always right.

Real hardware could only draw so many sprites on one scanline and simply dropped the rest, which is why characters flicker in busy moments. Removing the limit stops the flicker, at the cost of showing something the console never could.

Whether to show the blank margins around the picture that a television would have hidden behind its bezel. Off gives the clean image you probably expect; the others reveal what was really there, including the occasional glitchy edge column games never meant you to see.

The shape the core asks to be drawn at. Auto follows the region. NTSC/PAL PAR reproduce the non-square pixels of a real television, 4:3 is the classic TV shape, and Uncorrected shows square pixels — sharper, but slightly narrower than the artists drew for.

Imitates the way an NTSC television smeared and blended the picture over an aerial or composite lead. Several Mega Drive games relied on that blending to fake extra colours and transparency, most famously the waterfalls in Sonic — those look like coarse stripes without it.

Which model of the console\'s FM sound chip to emulate. The Mega Drive shipped with more than one revision and they genuinely sound different. The nuked options are far more accurate and cost noticeably more CPU; the mame ones are the sensible default.

Softens the harsh top end of the console’s output the way the real hardware’s analogue circuitry did. Low-pass is the faithful choice; EQ exposes manual bass/mid/treble instead. Off is the raw digital signal, which is cleaner but brighter than the console ever sounded.

Runs the emulated CPU faster than the real one to smooth out the slowdown some games shipped with. It is a hack — the games were written for the original speed — so expect glitches in anything that relied on the timing. Leave at 100 unless a specific game is struggling.

Some Lynx games were played with the console turned on its side, and the cartridge itself says which way. Auto reads that and rotates the picture to match, which is almost always what you want; the fixed choices exist for a ROM whose header is wrong. The core rotates the D-pad along with the screen, so up stays up whichever way the picture is facing.

Blends several frames together to imitate the real Lynx screen, whose LCD was slow enough that fast motion visibly smeared. More frames means a stronger effect and slightly more work per frame. Off is the sharp, modern-looking option — the Lynx never actually looked that clean.

How often the finished picture is handed to the display. The Lynx itself ran anywhere from 0 to 75Hz depending on what the game was doing, so this is a compromise: 60 matches most phone screens and is the safe choice, while 75 is closer to what the fastest games expected and can tear on a 60Hz panel.

Runs the emulated CPU faster than the real one, to smooth out slowdown that some games shipped with. This is a hack — the games were written for the original speed, and pushing past it can produce glitches or crashes. Leave at 1 unless a specific game is struggling.

Drops frames when the audio buffer is about to run dry, trading visual smoothness for sound that doesn\'t crackle. Auto skips only when the app says it is needed. Off is right unless you can hear crackling.

Blends each frame with the one before it. Some games flicker sprites on and off every frame — a trick that looked solid on the original LCD but strobes on a modern screen. The ghosting choices imitate that slow old screen more heavily.
Mutes the colours towards how they looked on the Game Boy Color\'s dim, unlit screen — games were drawn to look right there, so raw output can seem oversaturated.
Plays the original Nintendo start-up sequence — the falling logo and chime — before the game begins. Cosmetic only.
Lets Left and Right (or Up and Down) register at once — impossible on a real D-pad. A few games have tricks that need it; leave it off otherwise.

Speeds up the emulated SNES processor so scenes that slowed down on real hardware run smoothly. Not accurate to the original console, and it can break games that depend on the original timing — try \'light\' first.
How sound samples are smoothed as they play. \'gaussian\' is what the real SNES hardware did and is the authentic choice; the others sound crisper but aren\'t what the console produced.
Enables the SNES\'s higher-resolution and transparency modes, which games used for menus, text and effects. Turning it off is a speed hack that breaks those effects.
Whether to emulate a 60Hz NTSC console or a 50Hz PAL one. \'auto\' picks from the ROM — forcing the wrong one changes game speed and music pitch.
Raises the real console\'s limit on how many sprites fit on one scanline, so objects stop blinking out in busy scenes. Looks better, but isn\'t what the original hardware did.
Lets Left and Right (or Up and Down) register at once — impossible on a real D-pad. A few games have tricks that need it; leave it off otherwise.
How the emulated PlayStation processor is run. Recompiler is much the fastest and is the right choice normally; the interpreters are slower but more precise, worth trying only if a game misbehaves.
Renders in full colour depth instead of the PlayStation\'s 16-bit output, removing the visible banding in skies and gradients. Slightly less authentic, usually better-looking.

Games that ran in interlaced modes flicker line-by-line on a modern screen. Drawing them progressively instead is much steadier, and some render at a full 480p this way — but a few break outright, so turn it back on if a game glitches.
How much of the picture\'s edge to hide. Real TVs cut off the outermost pixels, and games often left junk out there. Borders trims it; None shows everything, including anything ugly at the edges.
Draws 3D geometry wider to fill a 16:9 screen instead of pillarboxing a 4:3 picture. Backgrounds, menus and pre-rendered scenes were drawn for 4:3, so those still look stretched.

The PlayStation scattered pixels in a fine pattern to fake extra colours and hide banding. \'1x(native)\' reproduces that speckled look exactly; \'internal resolution\' scales the pattern up with your resolution; \'disabled\' gives a clean image, but can expose colour banding unless Color Depth is set to 32bpp.
How many colours the renderer works in. 32bpp removes the banding the console\'s original 16-bit output shows on skies, gradients and video. 16bpp(native) is what the real hardware did.

How the disc image is read. \'sync\' reads on demand and is the safe choice; \'async\' reads ahead in the background; \'precache\' loads the whole disc into memory first — slower to start, but no loading hitches afterwards, provided there\'s RAM for it.
Speeds up the emulated CD drive so loading screens finish sooner. Anything above 2x(native) is faster than any real PlayStation, and games that assumed real disc timing can glitch or cut audio short.
Jumps straight into the game, skipping the PlayStation start-up logo. Some games and some memory-card behaviour depend on the real boot, so turn it off again if anything acts strangely.
Which regional console to emulate. \'auto\' works it out from the disc — only override it if a particular import refuses to run.
Gives the emulated graphics chip more drawing time per frame, which can clear up slowdown the original console suffered. Not accurate, and games tied to the original timing can glitch or run fast.
Speeds up the PlayStation\'s 3D maths unit, smoothing out framerate dips in heavy 3D scenes. Same trade-off as GPU Overclock — faster, less faithful.
\'disabled\' runs the emulated processor through the accurate but slower interpreter; \'execute\' switches on the fast dynamic recompiler. Faster is usually fine — switch back if a game misbehaves.
Skips processing sound channels that aren\'t actually audible. A free performance saving with nothing you can hear.
Skips redrawing the screen when nothing changed since the last frame, saving a little performance.
Draws 3D graphics at a multiple of the original resolution, so polygon edges look sharp instead of blocky. 2D backgrounds and pre-rendered art stay as they were. Higher settings cost performance.
Corrects texture alignment once Internal Resolution is above native, preventing thin seams and shimmering lines between texture tiles. Does nothing at 1x.

Smooths blocky textures. \'nearest\' is what the original hardware did; \'bilinear\' and \'3-point\' blur the pixels away; \'SABR\', \'xBR\' and \'JINC2\' try to reconstruct sharper detail instead, for more performance. Does nothing on the software renderer.

Some games draw effects out of very thin lines, which break up when rendered above native resolution. This widens them so they still show. \'aggressive\' catches more cases but can catch things it shouldn\'t.

Fixes the PlayStation\'s famous \'wobbly\' polygons — the real console had no sub-pixel precision, so geometry jitters and warps as it moves. \'memory only\' is the safer, faster half; \'memory + CPU\' corrects more but is heavier and upsets some games.
Uses PGXP\'s higher precision to work out which polygons are hidden, clearing up flicker and gaps its correction can otherwise introduce. Needs PGXP Geometry Correction switched on.
A speed-up for PGXP that reuses vertices it has already corrected. It can tighten up texture alignment, but a wrong match produces visible glitches — the core\'s own advice is to leave this off.
Fixes textures that visibly warp and swim across surfaces, floors and walls especially. Needs PGXP Geometry Correction switched on.
The shape of the picture. \'corrected\' shows it as it was meant to look on a period TV; \'uncorrected\' shows the raw pixels; the rest force a fixed shape regardless.
Real TVs hid the outermost edge of the picture, and games often left junk out there. \'smart\' trims only when there\'s something to trim; \'disabled\' shows everything, edge garbage included.

How to handle games that ran in interlaced modes, which flicker line-by-line on a modern screen. \'weave\' recombines both halves for full detail; \'bob\' avoids the comb-like tearing on fast motion, at some cost in sharpness.
Draws 3D geometry wider to fill a 16:9 screen instead of pillarboxing a 4:3 picture. Backgrounds, menus and pre-rendered scenes were drawn for 4:3, so those still look stretched.
How wide the Widescreen Hack stretches the 3D view. Does nothing unless Widescreen Hack is on.

Simulates the picture quality of a real cable running into a CRT. \'rgb\' is the sharpest; \'composite\' and \'rf\' progressively blur the image and add the colour artefacts old TVs produced — a CRT look without needing a shader.
Watches how far your analog sticks actually travel and adjusts the range it reports to the game, which helps sticks that don\'t quite reach full deflection.
Whether the emulated DualShock starts up in analog mode. Some games need analog on before they\'ll read the sticks; a few only behave correctly in digital mode.

SwanStation renders in software here, so its PGXP Geometry Correction and Texture Filtering options did nothing at all — they\'ve been removed rather than left sitting there looking like they work. Both need a hardware renderer, which is what the Beetle PSX HW core is for: switch the PS1 core to it under Graphics and you get real hardware rendering plus its own PGXP and texture-filtering options.
No core options for this system yet.

Uses a smaller audio buffer for less delay between pressing a button and hearing the result. Takes effect the next time a game is loaded. If you hear crackling or audio glitches on a particular game, try turning this off.
Star to auto-apply this preset every time a Pocket Taco connects
\"%1$s\" will auto-apply when Pocket Taco connects
Pocket Taco will reset to default bindings on connect

Restores your in-game save automatically whenever a ROM loads, and keeps it up to date whenever you leave the game (switch ROMs, open the library, or background the app). This is separate from save states — it\'s the same save data the game itself would write to a memory card or cartridge battery. Turn this off only if it causes trouble with a specific game.

PlayStation (PS1) games each get their own ~128KB virtual memory card, separate from every other PS1 game\'s. That\'s plenty of room for a normal playthrough — real PS1 memory cards hold far less and are shared across every game on them — but it isn\'t unlimited, so an especially save-heavy game could still fill it.

Logging in lets TacoBoy identify your games against RetroAchievements\' database, PS1 discs included. You can then open any recognised game\'s achievement list and see which ones you\'ve earned. Turn on Live Tracking below to have unlocks submitted automatically as you play — softcore only, as Hardcore Mode doesn\'t yet change how unlocks are reported. Long-press a game in the library and choose \"Check RetroAchievements\" to test whether a specific ROM is recognized.
Find this on your RetroAchievements profile\'s Settings page, under \"Keys\" — not your account password.

Unlocks achievements automatically as you play and reports them to RetroAchievements. Needs a separate login from the one above — RetroAchievements only accepts your account password (not the Web API key) for this. Your password is used once to sign in and is never stored; only the resulting session stays saved.

Disables the quick menu\'s save-state slots, per RetroAchievements\' Hardcore rules — your SRAM/cart save (auto-save and manual) is completely unaffected. This only hides the in-game save-state UI; it doesn\'t yet change how achievement unlocks are reported to RetroAchievements.
Connection failed — check your Web API key above
Couldn\'t sign in — check your username and password.
Controls how much detail is captured for Export Logs below. Always applies from the moment it\'s changed — nothing captured before that point can be recovered.

Every native library is 16 KB compatible, so TacoBoy runs normally on devices that use 16 KB memory pages, which newer Android hardware is moving to. Checked on each library as it ships, for segment alignment, segment layout and the RELRO segment, and confirmed on a 16 KB emulator, where the app launches without Android\'s compatibility warning. Not yet run on a 16 KB phone, since none has been available to test on.
No logs captured yet at the current log level
Restores every Settings tab to its defaults. Doesn\'t touch your RetroAchievements login, ROM folder, saved controller presets, or library (favorites, hidden games, custom titles).
This restores every Settings tab to its defaults. Your RetroAchievements login, ROM folder, controller presets, and library are unaffected. This can\'t be undone.
